abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The discovery of new antimicrobial drugs has become urgent due to the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance in the 21st century. However, high-throughput screening is costly and time-consuming. Artificial intelligence (AI) can facilitate the discovery of novel antibiotics and antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) by accelerating identification and reducing development costs. This review focuses on the application of artificial intelligence in the discovery of novel antibiotics and AMPs, highlighting recent advances and practical strategies in AI-driven antibacterial drug development. Ultimately, this article aims to provide practical support and guidance for researchers in antimicrobial discovery, thereby contributing to resolving the global health crisis.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The wide use of antibiotics has accelerated the spread of drug-resistant bacteria, leading to an increased infection rate. In the WHO European Region, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is directly responsible for 133 000 deaths each year and indirectly linked to 541 000 deaths [1]. Thus, infection by drug-resistant bacteria may become crucial, causing global death in the future and threatening human freedom, privacy, and health [2–4]. However, investment in antimicrobial drug research and development has declined, largely due to insufficient economic incentives and the absence of effective market mechanisms [5].

During the Golden Age of the 1940s, most antibiotics were discovered via the Waksman Platform [6]. The Waksman platform follows a workflow in which soil-derived bacteria are isolated, the colonies are screened for antibacterial activity, and the active secondary metabolites are subsequently purified. Although this approach has been highly successful for nearly two decades, challenges in the isolation and purification steps have made it less applicable in recent years [7]. Additionally, large libraries for screening antimicrobial agents [used as a general term referring to antibiotics and antimicrobial peptides (AMPs)] have limited chemical diversity for drug discovery, and no new antimicrobial agent classes have been discovered through this method since 1980 [8]. It is difficult to yield new scaffolds utilizing these traditional methods, and to avoid identifying known compounds.

In the past few decades, scientists have screened antimicrobial agents via a variety of strategies, such as natural product screening, high-throughput screening, evolutionary and phylogenetic analysis, structure-guided rational design, as well as new approaches such as the isolation chip (iChip) and resistance-guided discovery of new antibiotics [9, 10]. Virtual screening (VS) and molecular docking are also used because the above methods are extremely costly and time-consuming [11].

Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies have modernized the pharmaceutical field to accelerate antimicrobial agent discovery. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, such as protein structure prediction [12–14], virtual screening [15–19], toxicity prediction [20–22], pharmacophore modeling [23–26], drug repositioning [27–34], and clinical monitoring [35–46], have been applied to drug discovery. In these fields, they can reduce costs, increase efficiency, and improve the speed and accuracy of drug design. The structural characteristics of antibacterial agents tend to follow recognizable physicochemical and pharmacophoric patterns, making them recognizable and extractable using AI. The availability of large-scale antimicrobial datasets, including minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) values across diverse strains, provides essential data for an AI model. AI modeling offers a method of uncovering structure activity relationships from complex molecular and biological data. Predictive algorithms can rank candidate compounds based on antibacterial activity, while generative models expand the search space by designing new structures beyond those found in existing libraries. Through the integration of cheminformatics, bioactivity data, and modern machine learning techniques, these approaches contribute to more efficient identification of novel scaffolds and potential mechanisms of action.

Recent reviews have explored the growing role of AI in combating AMR. Researchers can now analyze large and complex datasets more efficiently, enabling the prediction of resistance trends, treatment responses, and infection outcomes [47, 48]. When applied to genomic data, ML algorithms can uncover genetic markers linked to antibiotic resistance, supporting the development of targeted treatment strategies [49]. In clinical settings, AI tools have shown promise in optimizing antimicrobial dosing and exploring novel therapies [47]. By integrating patient data with clinical outcomes, these technologies help diagnose infections more accurately and select appropriate therapies.

In addition, literature has increasingly explored the use of AI in antimicrobial research, with several reviews summarizing model design and methodological advances [50]. While these studies provide valuable insights into algorithmic development and performance evaluation, how such approaches could be translated into practical applications for discovering antimicrobial agents has received relatively less attention. To address this gap, we systematically summarize AI tools that have already led to experimentally validated antibiotic compounds and AMPs. By focusing on methodologies that integrate computational predictions with experimental feedback, this review aims to clarify how AI can be operationalized in real-world antimicrobial discovery. This review provides an overview of AI applications in antimicrobial agent development. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the practical applications of AI are discussed across key stages, including target validation, molecular discovery, AMPs discovery, and mechanism of action (MOA) prediction. In addition, this review compares the labeling strategies used in antimicrobial modeling to highlight challenges in model development and consistency.

sec.title: Data collection and dataset construction
sec.p: The quality of training data constrains the predictive performance of AI for drug discovery. The training data include publicly accessible small molecules and peptide structures, experimental activity values, such as MIC, half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50), and growth-inhibition percentages, and physicochemical or pharmacokinetic information. Data are usually collected from online databases such as ChEMBL [51], PubChem [52], and DrugBank [53], then manually processed to remove duplicate molecules, inorganic compounds, and mixtures. Finally, these data are used to construct the dataset.

The first step in pre-processing is to ensure consistent molecular representation by normalizing SMILES and InChI strings with RDKit or OpenBabel. Structures are standardized into a uniform format following public pipelines from ChEMBL and PubChem. After standardization, duplicates are collapsed using canonical identifiers. Activity records are harmonized by unit conversion, handling of censored values, aggregation of replicates, and removal of conflicting or low-quality assay entries [54]. Dataset splitting is performed based on the molecular scaffold rather than randomly to prevent leakage. For small molecules, the Bemis–Murcko scaffold split is usually performed, as it better captures inter-scaffold generalization and is adopted in benchmarks such as MoleculeNet [55].

Representations of small molecules are primarily derived from cheminformatics and include molecular graphs, SMILES strings, and molecular fingerprints, which capture atomic connectivity and substructures. AMPs are commonly represented based on sequence descriptors, including amino acid composition, physicochemical property vectors, k-mer embeddings, and learned sequence embeddings from deep learning models. The feature construction of AMPs refers to the transformation of primary amino acid sequences into numerical descriptors.

sec.title: Model selection and construction
sec.p: After constructing a dataset, model selection should balance predictive performance and computational efficiency. When datasets contain fewer compounds, traditional machine learning methods, including random forests (RF), support vector machines (SVM), and gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost), are reliable [56]. These models are more robust and allow some interpretations through feature importance measures and SHapley Additive explanation (SHAP) values [57].

When the database includes molecular structures or protein sequences on a larger scale, deep learning models perform better. Graph-based networks, such as graph convolutional networks (GCNs), capture local atomic interactions, and graph attention networks (GATs) emphasize context-dependent features, often compared with known pharmacophores [58]. For peptide or protein sequences, models based on Transformer architectures, including bidirectional encoder representation from transformers (BERT) variants, can capture long-range residue interactions. Combined with specific position scoring matrices, these models have demonstrated better performance in AMPs.

In generative modeling for molecular design, frameworks such as variational autoencoders (VAEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and autoregressive language models are widely applied. VAEs map molecules into a continuous latent space suitable for optimization, and GANs and language models can generate novel structures to explore novel chemical space. These generators are often combined with complex scoring functions that incorporate drug-likeness, toxicity, and synthetic accessibility to perform multiple iterations.

Finally, large language models pre-trained on massive molecular or protein sequence databases (e.g. ChemBERTa, MolBERT, and ProtGPT2) have provided a base for fine-tuning [59, 60]. Fine-tuning these models on antimicrobial datasets has been shown to improve performance, particularly in low-data settings, while also reducing the complexity of hyperparameter tuning.

sec.title: Model training and evaluation
sec.p: Reliable evaluation is critical for training the model. A common evaluation approach is to divide the dataset into training, validation, and test sets based on random splits or scaffold splitting strategies. However, both approaches have some issues. Random splits often leak duplicates and reward memorization, while scaffold splits can still carry hidden bias [55, 61]. To address these issues, robust validation is used within the training data. K-fold cross-validation is commonly used for hyperparameter tuning, ensuring that evaluation is more reliable across different data partitions. In the meantime, stratified sampling helps maintain balanced class distributions, particularly in imbalanced classification tasks.

The Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC-AUC) can look deceptively strong under class imbalance, whereas the Precision–Recall Area Under the Curve (PR-AUC) is more informative, ideally presented with confidence intervals via bootstrapping [55]. Accuracy, recall, specificity, and the F₁ score complement the evaluation metrics, based on the practical requirements of the task. A better method is to predefine the decision threshold and combine it with the wet-lab result. In regression tasks predicting MIC or IC50 values, metrics include root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and Pearson or Spearman correlation. Because these metrics alone cannot reveal how model performance scales with available data, learning curve analysis is recommended to systematically quantify data requirements [62]. By training the model on a larger dataset, learning curves reveal whether performance has plateaued or whether the dataset remains insufficient. Furthermore, transfer learning and multitask pretraining can reduce the amount of task-specific labeled data required, because shared representations learned from prediction tasks often improve efficiency [63].

Graph neural networks may rely on statistical regularities to distinguish training and test data. Models may effectively memorize features of the split rather than learning SAR. Generative models need to reduce overfitting and avoid generating misleading outputs. Some work demonstrates that many of the model’s benchmarks reward memorization instead of generalization. Yet, generative pipelines can easily collapse even while continuing to perform very well on the validity and novelty metrics [61]. Community benchmarks could be used to improve generalization ability, such as GuacaMol and MOSES. While MOSES and GuacaMol have played an important role in standardizing evaluation and improving reproducibility, these metrics do not directly measure extrapolative performance in bioactivity prediction. There is a gap between benchmark performance and real-world utility, and benchmark results should be interpreted with appropriate caution.

All in all, it is the combination of good-quality data, appropriate model choices, and rigorous evaluation that will lead to performance in computational antimicrobial discovery. As datasets continue to grow larger and improve in quality, and as models continue to improve, there is an increasing possibility of more efficient identification of novel compounds and AMPs.

sec.title: The application of AI in antimicrobial drug discovery
Predicting the structure of the antimicrobial target
sec.p: AI can be used to predict the 3D structure of targets, and is one of the most popular tools, AlphaFold [64]. AlphaFold is an ML-based tool for predicting the 3D structures of proteins on the basis of their amino acid sequences [65]. The process consists of two main steps. First, the tool uses convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to convert the amino acid sequence into a distance matrix and a torsion angle matrix. Second, a gradient optimization technique transforms these matrices into the final 3D structure [66]. The accuracy of the 3D structure of the target determines the validity of the virtual screening result, which can be used to select drug candidates rapidly and efficiently for activity assays [67]. For this purpose, Bader et al. used AlphaFold2 (Fig. 2) and subtractive genome analysis to predict the 3D structure of the Vibrio vulnificus strain ATCC 27562 drug target [68]. The molecule ZINC01318774 (Fig. 4), which binds to the binding pocket of bisphosphoglycerate-independent phosphoglycerate mutase, was subsequently identified via virtual screening and molecular docking experiments. As mentioned, the accurate target structure models generated by AlphaFold2 build a good foundation for virtual screening based on molecular docking.

sec.title: Predicting the antimicrobial activity of molecules
sec.p: Recently, the use of molecular representations and neural networks has significantly increased antibacterial molecule screening. Jonathan M et al. trained a directed-message passing neural network model called Chemprop with a collection of 2560 molecules selected for their ability to inhibit Escherichia coli BW25113 growth [8]. The model predicted antibacterial activity by identifying 51 active compounds out of 99 candidates from the Drug Repurposing Hub, with an OD600 < 0.2 growth inhibition cut-off. Notably, the molecule Halicin (Fig. 4) was also found to be effective at inhibiting Clostridioides difficile and panresistant Acinetobacter baumannii infections in murine models, suggesting that it could be a broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent.

Guo X et al. identified a compound against Helicobacter pylori via a deep graph neural network (Attentive Fingerprint) (Fig. 3), with over 13 000 molecules [69]. This method resulted in a new berberine derivative that shows strong activity toward both drug-sensitive and drug-resistant strains. Chemoproteomic analysis confirmed that the compound specifically targets the bacterial outer membrane protein transport and assembly machinery, specifically SecA and BamD.

caption.p: Attentive fingerprint general framework. The framework begins with a molecular structure represented as a graph, where atoms are nodes and chemical bonds are edges. Through a directed message passing mechanism with attention weighting, the model learns representations for each atom by aggregating information from its neighbors weighted by attention scores. The framework consists of multiple attention-based layers that first update atomic embeddings, followed by molecule-level embedding layers that aggregate atomic features into a fixed molecular fingerprint. This learned representation is then passed through a task layer to predict molecular properties, such as antimicrobial activity.

graphic.alt-text: Schematic of the attentive fingerprint framework, where a molecular graph is processed by attention-based message passing to generate atomic embeddings, aggregate them into a molecular fingerprint, and predict properties.

sec.p: However, GNNs are difficult to interpret because they are ‘black box’ models. Wong et al. applied an interpretative machine learning pipeline that combines GNNs with Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to identify substructure-level rationales for antimicrobial activity [10]. Novel chemical scaffolds for antimicrobial agents were identified via this method, one of which is of particular interest. The new scaffold was not only found to have high selectivity and good toxicological profiles but was also effective against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) in mouse models. This study demonstrated the potential of a graph-based neural network to enhance predictive performance.

AI is also used to design narrow-spectrum antimicrobial agents that target specific pathogens. Liu et al. screened ~7500 molecules (FDA-approved drugs and compounds from the Broad Institute) that use the growth of A. baumannii to create a training dataset [70]. They trained a neural network to predict structural compounds with antimicrobial activity of the agent against A. baumannii. Ultimately, they identified abaucin (Fig. 4), which demonstrates narrow-spectrum activity by perturbing lipoprotein trafficking via a mechanism involving LolE.

sec.p: ChemLM is a transformer-based language model for identifying antimicrobials against the growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa [71]. The training of the model consists of three main parts: (i) self-supervised pretraining, (ii) domain-specific pretraining, and (iii) fine-tuning for molecular property prediction. Domain self-adaptation is one of the important innovations that allows pretrained models to be trained on more data to capture specific structures and improve performance. ChemLM utilizes the SMILES enumeration technique to generate alternative sequence representations of molecules, thereby increasing the number of training instances. Hyper-parametric optimization shows that the type of embedding and the number of enhancements in domain adaptation have a significant impact on model performance. During the supervised fine-tuning phase, ChemLM chose not to freeze all layers of the Transformer and fine-tuned them to optimize performance. Compared to other language models such as MolBERT and MolFormer, ChemLM demonstrates superior performance on the highly unbalanced ClinTox dataset. Finally, ChemLM was successfully applied to real-world datasets with a limited number of samples to identify antimicrobials against P. aeruginosa.

sec.title: Generating the molecules
sec.p: Although ML approaches have been valuable in predicting antimicrobial properties for drug screening, a significant challenge remains in discovering novel antimicrobial structures. This is largely because most ML algorithms rely on human-defined features for learning and prediction [72]. As a result, these predefined features limit the exploration of truly innovative and unexplored chemical structures with potential antimicrobial activity. Generative models offer a solution to this problem by enabling the generation of new molecules. These models include various types, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), autoencoders (AEs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and transformers, which can create novel chemical structures that may have antimicrobial properties [73].

Generative AI has proven effective in exploring vast chemical spaces and predicting the properties of potential antimicrobial candidates. For example, Swanson et al. developed SyntheMol, a platform that combines generative AI with property prediction models to discover new antimicrobial agents [74]. SyntheMol uses real-world data to assess the chemical space of potential molecules, which is further explored by generative AI models. The researchers trained a model to predict antimicrobial activity using a dataset of ~13 000 molecules from growth inhibition assays against A. baumannii. After the synthesis and testing of 58 structurally unique compounds, six showed novel structures (Fig. 4) and antimicrobial activity. These compounds demonstrated broad-spectrum efficacy against various gram-negative bacteria, including A. baumannii, E. coli, and Klebsiella pneumoniae.

Recent research increasingly incorporates synthetic complexity scores and in silico retrosynthetic analysis. The Synthetic Accessibility Score (SAscore) can be integrated into generative modeling to enable models to generate chemically realistic and synthesizable scaffolds [75]. The integration of AI tools has further strengthened the ability to filter and optimize de novo designs by providing synthetic routes in the early stages of generation. As a result, modern generative models are moving toward jointly optimizing both bioactivity and synthetic feasibility.

sec.title: Predicting the antimicrobial activity of AMPs
sec.p: Researchers have used protein sequence and antimicrobial activity data to train models for predicting and identifying potential AMPs [76]. However, the application of AI in the identification of AMPs remains challenging because of their complexity. Torres et al. developed a scoring function based on physicochemical properties, including net charge, average hydrophobicity, and sequence length, to predict potential AMPs from the human proteome [77]. With this scoring function, they identified 2600 potential AMPs from a dataset of 42 361 sequences. Thirty-five synthesized peptides showed antimicrobial activity against pathogenic bacterial species.

Shorter hexapeptides are potentially useful as AMPs since they are simpler to use clinically, although they tend to exhibit lower antimicrobial activity compared to longer peptide sequences [78, 79]. Huang et al. trained a machine learning pipeline on three different databases—the UniProt database, an external dataset of GrAMPsa, and an internal dataset of experimentally validated peptides—to predict potent AMPs [80]. A data-driven plug-and-play machine-learning approach for identifying the best hexapeptide candidates from an extremely large search space is described in this research. To avoid potential biases from a single model, the framework combines multiple models to expand the hypothesis space, using a stagewise funnel-like pipeline. The approach begins with an empirical prefiltering step, removing peptides that do not meet specific structural criteria, and reducing the candidate pool to 3.93 million peptides. The pipeline then applies a classification module for robust, rough predictions, followed by a ranking module to assess antibacterial activity, and concludes with a regression module for precise MIC value predictions. The approach balances prediction granularity with robustness against dataset noise and bias. The results demonstrated the antimicrobial activity of the identified AMPs against clinical multidrug-resistant pathogens in the identified AMPs. In addition, aerosolized formulations of the AMPs had similar therapeutic potency to penicillin, low toxicity, and little ability to promote drug resistance.

Recent advancements in AI have significantly altered the process of discovering and designing of antimicrobial agents. With the application of machine learning, AI can sift through vast amounts of data, identify patterns, and forecast. One of the most beneficial features of AI is that it can predict the antibacterial activity of compounds by examining their molecular patterns. AI is not just applied to small-molecule antimicrobial agents, but it has also significantly impacted the field of AMPs, which hold the potential to serve as a better alternative to traditional antimicrobial agents, particularly in the context of increasing antimicrobial resistance. AI algorithms have been used to predict and design AMPs based on protein sequences and physicochemical features, overcoming some of them by choosing peptides that have antimicrobial activity. Methods such as scoring functions, ranking methods, and regression models enable scientists to refine estimates and identify candidates with the greatest potential therapeutic value.

sec.title: Genomic mining of AMPs
sec.p: Genomic mining of AMPs is an emerging trend, driven by the urgent need for new antibiotics against the growing crisis of antibiotic resistance. It primarily involves the use of computational approaches, such as ML and DL, which are applied to vast global datasets [81].

The AMPSphere [82] is an open-access resource designed to accelerate the discovery of novel AMPs. This resource is based on a large-scale database integrated with ML models. Researchers utilized a comprehensive global dataset comprising 63 410 metagenomes and 87 920 high-quality prokaryotic genomes from various environmental and host-associated habitats. The prediction of candidate AMPs (c_AMPs) was based on Macrel [83], a machine learning pipeline that employs random forests and prioritizes precision over recall in identifying AMPs from extensive peptide datasets. AMPSphere was constructed use Macrel, which includes 863 498 non-redundant c_AMPs from previously described databases. For experimental validation, 100 AMP candidates were synthesized and tested for activity against clinically drug-resistant pathogens and human gut commensals using both in vitro and in vivo platforms. The results demonstrated that 79 active peptides were identified. Furthermore, lead candidates showed activity in a mouse infection model. Notably, AMPSphere identified nearly one million c_AMPs, 91.5% of which were previously unknown. Most importantly, the identified AMPs are effective against drug-resistant pathogens.

Based on the attentive DL model AMPlify [84], c_AMPs precursor sequences were identified in target genomes via homology search and genome annotation tools. These precursor sequences were then subjected to in silico cleavage at the C-terminal side of conserved enzymatic motifs, including the lysine–arginine signal found in amphibian precursors, to generate putative mature peptide sequences consisting of 200 or fewer amino acid residues. The resulting sequences were subsequently analyzed by the AMPlify model, which utilizes a Bi-LSTM layer and attention mechanisms to process sequence information and generate a probability score. Sequences with scores above 0.5 were classified as putative AMPs. To prioritize c_AMPs for experimental validation, AMPs were filtered according to physicochemical properties to enhance structural stability and facilitate chemical synthesis. This approach successfully identified novel AMPs with broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity against a wide range of bacterial isolates.

However, several challenges remain in AI-based discovery of AMPs from genomics and transcriptomics. These include the technical difficulty of distinguishing genuine protein-coding sequences from false positives in genomic analyses, the limited quantity of detailed AMP sequence data available for ML model training, and potential biases from global habitats in public databases [82]. Nonetheless, these AI models also yield functional AMPs that exhibit potent anti-infective activity in preclinical models.

sec.title: Generating the AMPs
sec.p: Das et al. used a deep autoencoder to design an AMP generative model that includes an encoder and a decoder. In their study, they explored the efficacy of variational autoencoder (VAE) and wasserstein autoencoder (WAE) models in generating peptide sequences [79]. The VAE functions by assuming a simple prior distribution for latent variables, which is then used by the decoder to generate sequences. In contrast, the WAE aims to learn a more robust representation by minimizing the Wasserstein distance between the true and generated distributions in the latent space [85]. Peptide generation is considered a density modeling problem with a focus on modeling the distribution of peptide sequences to generate new high-likelihood sequences [79]. The model was then trained on a set of labeled peptide sequences and leveraged large-scale unlabeled peptide data through training on this scale to acquire the syntactic and structural characteristics of peptide sequences and navigate the vaster sequence space. Upon testing, the outcome validates the superiority of WAE in peptide sequence generation by demonstrating its ability to learn the relationships in sequences, preserve functional characteristics, and create new sequences with high efficiency. Then, they filtered the designed AMPs through molecular dynamics simulations deep-learning classifiers and physicochemical descriptors derived from high-throughput molecular dynamics simulations. Finally, the wet experiment results revealed that two out of the 20 AMPs had high effectiveness against pathogens and a low propensity to induce drug resistance in E. coli.

In addition, Ma et al. built a pipeline for AMP identification via multiple neural network models, including long short-term memory (LSTM), attention layers, and BERT [86]. This approach improved accuracy and reduced false positives, achieving a precision of 91.31%. The experimental results revealed that 181 of the 216 synthesized peptides exhibited antimicrobial activity, with several candidates demonstrating strong efficacy against antimicrobial-resistant gram-negative pathogens in a mouse model.

ML techniques, while effective in predicting antimicrobial properties, are strongly reliant on human-designed features, which limits the exploration of new chemical spaces. Generative AI models offer an enriching alternative by enabling the creation of new molecular structures with antimicrobial activity. Generative AI models can explore rich chemical spaces, predict the properties of potential drug candidates, and generate new compounds that may be overlooked by traditional methods.

sec.title: Predicting the antimicrobial mechanism-of-action
sec.p: It is necessary to explore the MOA of antimicrobial agents for drug design, and many strategies can contribute to interpreting the MOA [87]. Espinoza et al. trained a CoHEC model through whole-transcriptome responses on the basis of a hierarchical ensemble of classifiers model and Clairvoyance to interpret the MOA [88]. They analyzed transcriptome responses from Escherichia, including 41 known antimicrobial agents and nine crude extracts, contributing 122 unique transcriptomes to this study. The CoHEC model showed exceptional accuracy, predicting the primary MOA for previously unobserved compounds—including both purified forms and crude extracts—with over 99% accuracy. It also correctly identified darobactin as a novel MOA. Additionally, when applied to recent transcriptomics and metabolomics datasets from different bacterial strains, the method was better than the metrics reported in original publications. The results suggested that MOA analysis can cover a broad spectrum of effects through a variety of compounds.

An innovative study recently revealed that the use of ML models in antimicrobial agent discovery can be interpreted. Wong et al. identified substructure rationales for compounds with high predicted antimicrobial activity and low predicted cytotoxicity through graph algorithms [10, 89]. In this work, the authors combined GNNs with MCTS to interpret the ‘black-box’ logic of deep learning models and complete a full experimental validation. A GNN first embeds molecules as graphs to predict their probabilities of exhibiting antibacterial activity. MCTS is then used to remove peripheral bonds or rings to identify the minimal substructures that retain high predicted activity, thereby enhancing interpretability. Experimental validation demonstrated that the 283 compounds containing these minimal substructures exhibited antibacterial activity, confirming the prediction. Microscopic imaging, ΔpH monitoring, and pH-dependent assays revealed disruption of the proton motive force as the compounds’ mechanism of action. Resistance evolution and whole-genome sequencing experiments indicated low risk of resistance development. Finally, candidate compounds demonstrated vivo efficacy and safety in murine infection models. This study establishes a complete pipeline from model interpretability to mechanistic validation and in vivo efficacy. This method facilitates the discovery of new classes of antimicrobial agents via interpretative machine learning (IML), especially in identifying important chemical substructures for antimicrobial activity.

Understanding the MOA of antimicrobial agents is central to drug development optimization, and AI is increasingly being used to optimize the process. One fascinating application has been for the use of machine learning algorithms in the analysis of transcriptomic data, with researchers being able to accurately predict the MOA of several antimicrobial agents, including new molecules, with high success. The AI-based provides a more general analysis of antimicrobial activity against different bacterial strains. In addition, AI contributes to the identification of new classes of antimicrobial agents by improving data interpretability. By graph-based analysis, researchers have been successful in identifying critical substructures within compounds related to high antimicrobial activity and low cytotoxicity. This interpretative strategy not only helps identify novel classes of antimicrobial agents but also provides valuable information about their structural characteristics. The ability to analyze large datasets and uncover hidden patterns is driving innovation in antimicrobial agents so that the emerging challenge of antimicrobial resistance can be addressed.

sec.title: Predicting ADMET properties
sec.p: The application of AI in ADMET property prediction has offered a data-driven alternative to traditional methods that are expensive and time-consuming. AI-based methods help to address the high attrition rate in drug development.

ADMET prediction platforms can be divided into three categories [90]. First, rule-based/statistical methods, such as Swiss ADME and SMARTCyp 3.0, rely on predefined rules. Second, conventional ML methods, represented by ProTox 3.0, use algorithms like Random Forest to improve predictive accuracy [91]. Third, the latest graph-based methods leverage Graph Neural Networks and are represented by tools such as admetSAR 3.0 and ADMETlab 3.0. These methods automatically extract complex molecular features and often provide superior predictive performance. In addition, Large Language Models demonstrate great potential in automated literature mining (e.g. UniTox) and in constructing high-quality ADMET benchmark datasets (e.g. PharmaBench) [92].

Despite these advances, important challenges persist, such as heterogeneous and incomplete data quality, difficulties in modeling novel or complex multi-target compounds, and the use of ‘black-box’ models that limit biological interpretability and regulatory acceptance [93]. Further progress in computational methods is expected to depend on multi-level and multi-omics integration, combining data from chemical structure, gene expression, and metabolomics into model construction. All in all, AI in ADMET prediction has evolved from low-throughput methods to automated solutions. Classic approaches offer precise predictions but are limited in speed and scope, while ML and graph-based models rapidly explore large chemical spaces. Moreover, LLMs integrate literature with data context into actionable safety knowledge. These advancements can help screen antimicrobial compounds and AMPs.

sec.title: Ethical AI frameworks for applications
sec.p: In January 2025, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) released the draft guidance ‘Considerations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence to Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products.’ The guidance requires sponsors of AI systems to submit an interpretability dossier that classifies model architecture, data provenance, and feature-attribution analyses. It introduces a risk-adapted Credibility Assessment Framework, which classifies AI tools into low, medium, and high-risk tiers and prescribes validation evidence. The FDA also encourages pre-IND meetings such that experimental design, evaluation metrics, and post-marketing monitoring plans are suitable for the framework. In June 2025, the FDA issued its guidance entitled ‘Antibacterial Therapies for Patients with an Unmet Medical Need.’ These initiatives demonstrate that high-need antimicrobial therapies are moving toward more flexible regulatory pathways.

In addition to these regulatory efforts, other policies have emerged, such as the Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) principles and the FDA’s internal AI tool, Elsa, which was launched in 2025. Elsa requires continuous performance monitoring and allows for the explanation of interactive model submissions during regulatory review. In the pharmaceutical industry, Eli Lilly partnered with OpenAI in 2024 to accelerate the development of new antibiotics. This collaboration demonstrates how partnerships between pharmaceutical and AI companies are advancing antibacterial pipelines.

sec.title: Discussion on difference of label variables in AI models
sec.p: AI-based drug discovery is more economical and effective [44]. The process starts from target identification where AI helps detect genes or proteins associated with disease [94]. Through virtual screening and lead optimization, the efficacy is improved, and toxicity is minimized, often via quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models and pharmacophore modeling [95]. Additionally, drug release monitoring ensures that drugs are used at appropriate dosages and released effectively. Finally, AI can contribute to optimizing clinical trials by analyzing data to identify the most effective treatments and dosages [96]. However, in the stage of activity prediction, antimicrobial agents differ from other drugs.

In antibacterial agents discovery, growth-inhibitory activity is used to screen for bacteriostat compounds. Purely target-based screening is generally adjusted to antimicrobial drug discovery [97]. Growth-inhibitory activity measures the lowest concentration of a compound that inhibits bacterial growth, reflecting its antimicrobial properties [98]. The growth-inhibitory activity is more phenotypic, including almost all effects on bacterial populations. In contrast, target-based screening reveals the concentration at which a compound inhibits 50% of its target enzyme or receptor, more focusing on biochemical interactions at the molecular level [99]. Therefore, growth-inhibitory activity accounts for more complex biological factors. In contrast, the IC50 reflects only antibacterial molecular targets​.

The ability of the AI to predict antibacterial activity is mainly based on the growth-inhibitory activity values of the antimicrobial agents [100]. The growth-inhibitory activity values, such as cell wall permeability, efflux pump activity, and biofilms, all of which can impact antibacterial activity, are associated with target-based screening losses. Target-based methods do depend on a unique molecular target, e.g. an enzyme or receptor. Another reason to employ growth-inhibitory activity values for prediction is the rapid evolution of bacterial resistance mechanisms. Growth inhibitory activity can be used to identify compounds that act against resistant strains. This technique allows the identification of drugs to circumvent mechanisms of resistance, e.g. target binding site changes.

In comparison, target-based screening may miss these compounds. This technique focuses more on a specific target, without considering the complex mechanism of bacterial resistance [101] Moreover, growth-inhibitory activity values evaluate whole-cell activity, offering an extensive view of antibacterial factors. Multiple bacterial pathways and physiological systems are considered. A targeting drug might not yield the same effect in a bacterial system, including complex pathways. Some antimicrobial agents exhibit antibacterial activity through multiple targets or unknown targets [102]. Growth-inhibitory activity value evaluation does not require knowledge of these targets, making it a more flexible approach. This is especially valuable in the discovery of novel antibacterial compounds with unknown mechanisms of action. Additionally, many successful antimicrobial agents affect multiple pathways, which are likely missed in traditional target-based screening [103]. Finally, the evaluation of growth-inhibitory activity values more accurately simulates real conditions, with the testing conditions considering environmental factors and clinical infections. Although target-based screening is used to identify biochemical interactions, it cannot cover the antibacterial system, where drug effectiveness is influenced by complex environmental and bacterial factors. Thus, growth-inhibitory activity values are commonly used to construct datasets to train models for predicting antibacterial activity.

The use of growth-inhibitory activity in ML models of antibacterial drug discovery offers significant advantages, but it also presents several limitations (As shown in Table 1). Growth-inhibitory activity values are derived from phenotypic assays, which evaluate the overall effect of a compound on a biological system. While it covers a wide range, the complexity of the environmental factors produces considerable variability in the data. Factors such as bacterial strain type, growth conditions, and experimental protocols can cause inconsistent or noisy data. The model may learn irrelevant factors, leading to inaccurate predictions when applied to new data. Data based on growth-inhibitory activity reduce the interpretability of the model [10]. Since growth-inhibitory activity provides a phenotypic analysis without the mechanisms of action, the model might neglect the functions of specific biochemical interactions or pathways. This lack makes it difficult to interpret why a compound inhibits bacterial growth and resistance mechanisms, limiting the interpretability of the model. The growth-inhibitory activity is highly dependent on the experimental conditions. The bacterial inoculum size, incubation time, and composition of the growth medium may impact the results. The results related to specific laboratory conditions make it difficult to ensure that growth-inhibitory activity values are comparable across different studies. These inconsistencies may lead to model overfitting factors, leading to the neglect of crucial bacterial features. Overall, growth-inhibitory activity data are valuable for analyzing the phenotypic effects of compounds in real biological systems. However, these limitations reduce data variability and interpretability, making it difficult to build robust and interpretable ML models. These limitations also neglect mechanisms of action, which are critical for understanding drug efficacy and resistance.

sec.p: To overcome these drawbacks and improve reliability, a systematic strategy for reducing batch variability and standardizing dataset generation is required. It is a method to decrease the variability between different experimental batches by adopting a normalization procedure based on quality control [104]. Each batch should contain reference bacterial strains whose MICs serve as internal standards to correct batch differences. Data collection should be performed according to the protocol provided by the European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST), which standardizes the selection of strains, the preparation of inoculum, incubation time, and determination of the endpoint. In theory, the federated learning framework could enable model training across several institutions based on the above methods. Accordingly, we outlined an integrated protocol including standardized data collection, calibration across datasets, and federated model training (Fig. 5). Current normalization strategies are not always sufficient for AI models. The biases cannot be fully addressed by simple normalization or standardization protocols. While these procedures may reduce such discrepancies, they are insufficient to eliminate them. At present, there is no consensus for resolving this question.

caption.p: Overview of the standardized data collection, cross-dataset calibration, and federated learning workflow. The framework consists of three protocol modules. Standardized data collection includes (i) strain selection using a defined panel with at least two reference strains per batch to monitor variability, (ii) inoculum preparation with photometric density standardization, (iii) controlled incubation following established guidelines, (iv) endpoint determination using photometric MIC readings performed by two blinded observers, and (v) comprehensive data logging of strain ID, lot number, incubation parameters, instrumentation, and operator information. Cross-dataset calibration incorporates internal QC reference strains in every batch to quantify deviation from expected MIC values and trains a correction model using QC strain data to remove batch biases. Federated learning uses a model framework such as Chemprop with federated averaging. Each institution performs local MIC standardization and batch correction, while QC strain results are shared across sites to harmonize baselines. Final validation is conducted using an external evaluation dataset.

sec.p: In addition, the combination of growth-inhibitory activity data and biological information could help address these questions. By combining growth-inhibitory activity data with genomic, proteomic, and metabolic data, ML models can be used to understand both the outcomes and the mechanisms of action. This approach could enhance both the predictive accuracy and interpretability of models, leading to better drug candidate selection and a deeper understanding of resistance mechanisms. In summary, while growth-inhibitory activity is an essential component of antibacterial drug screening, we should also focus on the combination of phenotypic data with mechanisms of action, making models more precise and more interpretable in the future.

sec.title: Shortage and future
sec.p: Antimicrobial compound design has increasingly leveraged AI. Many approaches primarily utilize drug databases to train ML models; however, they often do not verify computational predictions with wet-lab experiments [105]. The critical distinction among such studies typically lies in the choice of the database. For example, Liu et al. enhanced the predictive accuracy of their model by reforming an antimicrobial activity database, which included screening for growth inhibition against specific bacteria [70]. Therefore, the primary challenge remains the accuracy of the target variable used in supervised learning, underscoring the necessity of experimental validation to confirm the success of these computational approaches. Melo et al. reviewed research trends on the basis of PubMed data, comparing the progress in antimicrobial agent discovery to developments in other therapeutic areas, such as cancer and cardiovascular treatments [106]. The results indicate a growing interest in all fields; however, research on antimicrobial agents specifically demonstrates a notable shortage. In addition, IC50 values for drug targets are also employed. However, this approach is infrequently used in the training of models for antimicrobial drugs. The limited use is largely attributed to the scarcity of data on target-based antimicrobial drugs, which primarily stems from how many antimicrobials were discovered in the last century—often through the screening of bacterial secondary metabolites. As a result, many antimicrobial drugs lack defined specific targets and associated data, posing significant challenges for training models that use IC50 values as target variables. Moreover, the computational resources required to train DL models are another bottleneck. Many reported models rely on extensive Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) resources, large memory capacities, and long training times. These resources may not be accessible to most academic laboratories. The disparity in computational resources can limit model reproducibility and practical application. Therefore, recent research has increasingly explored transfer learning and the reuse of pre-trained foundation models.

The future of antimicrobial agent discovery, which will be greatly enhanced by ML over the next decade, lies in improved data availability. As more datasets become accessible, they will contribute to the exploration of new ML questions and permit a more rigorous reevaluation of existing queries. The critical factor is the expansion of publicly available experimental data, which allows for the growth of datasets across institutions without compromising private data [107]. The method to increase data sharing from pharmaceutical projects—both successful and failed—aims to accelerate research and development [108]. Moreover, the reanalysis of existing data for new purposes revealed the potential to repurpose nonantimicrobial agents for antimicrobial use, a prospect already advanced by deep learning techniques [109].

Continued collaboration among fields such as computer science, biology, and medicine is crucial [110]. This approach not only enhances the technical accuracy of biomedical ML studies but also promises similar benefits for computational antimicrobial agent discovery [111]. This collaborative approach promotes the integration of computational predictions with empirical laboratory validations, aiming to produce robust, actionable results. IML aims to mitigate the opacity of traditional ML models by making their decision-making processes more transparent and interpretable [10]. This is particularly valuable in elucidating the MOA of antimicrobial agents, thereby enhancing understanding and facilitating further research.

There is no doubt that ML and DL can accelerate the speed of antimicrobial agent discovery, but the accuracy of AI predictions is debatable. Consequently, in this review, AI applications in the identification and screening of novel antibiotics and AMPs are introduced, following the logical progression of drug discovery from target prediction to MOA prediction. Additionally, the examples presented are experimentally validated by antimicrobial tests and have some application and value.

Recent advances in antimicrobial compound design have increasingly utilized artificial intelligence, training machine learning models with drug databases, although these often lack verification through wet laboratory experiments. The key issue is the accuracy of the target variables and the necessity for experimental validation [70]. To address this gap, we systematically summarize AI tools that have already led to experimentally validated antibiotic compounds and AMPs (Table 2). In the discovery of halicin, the researchers chose growth inhibition as the biological property because it easily generates reproducible data [8]. Although the screen based on growth inhibition made it difficult to clarify the mechanism of action, future applications can incorporate phenotypic conditions that enrich molecules against specific targets. In addition, research on halicin still lacks optimization of drug-like properties and clinical research.

sec.p: Research comparing antimicrobial agent discovery to other fields shows a lag in research on antimicrobial agents, with challenges including data scarcity for target-based drugs discovered primarily through historical screening methods [112]. The future of antimicrobial agent discovery lies in improved data availability and sharing, with the potential for repurposing nonantimicrobial agents. Interdisciplinary collaboration is crucial for integrating computational predictions with empirical validations, and there is a focus on making ML models more transparent and interpretable to better understand mechanisms of action. Most importantly, we must develop a comprehensive and effective pipeline that integrates artificial intelligence with antimicrobial drug design.
